A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VILA research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison despite reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original eight-benchmark evaluations, online-learning experiments, component ablations, case studies and efficiency measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds rank-sensitivity, computational-budget, extended component-ablation and backbone-replacement experiments.

M1.justification: The dual-branch architecture, UGC, CSE and recursive learning procedure remain unchanged. Appendix B.2.1 adds an offline-caching deployment variant, called VILA-SOC elsewhere: Algorithms 3–4 precompute class text prototypes and replace inference-time text encoding with lookup, allowing the text encoder to be offloaded.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight datasets and recognition tasks. The added ablations and computational controls reuse this coverage; different task counts and backbones change experimental settings rather than represented domains or task requirements.

E2.justification: TUNA replaces EASE in the benchmark and online comparisons in Tables 2–3 and in the corresponding accuracy and efficiency plots. The other baseline identities are retained; larger and dual-backbone RanPAC/LoRanPAC configurations serve as additional experimental controls.

E3.justification: The original benchmark protocols remain, but v2 adds substantial evaluation designs: a five-rank LoRA sweep, FLOP/parameter measurements, approximately matched-compute and larger-backbone controls, and DINOv2 substitution without CSE. Table 8 also evaluates components under additional task-count configurations within the retained datasets.

E4.justification: New analyses investigate LoRA collapse across ranks (Table 5), capacity as an explanation for gains (Tables 6–7), component contributions on six further datasets (Table 8), and dependence on CLIP through DINOv2 replacement (Table 9). The existing K-sensitivity analysis is retained and moved to Appendix D.3.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same five global seeds, {1993, 1, 56, 254, 602}, and retain the existing ± reporting in Tables 3–4. No new uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test or explicit increase in repeated runs is documented.

E6.justification: Tables 5–9 add substantial numerical evidence for rank sensitivity, computational cost, controlled comparisons and ablations. For example, Table 5 reports 88.91/93.03 accuracy for rank-16 ViT-LoRA on CIFAR with 20 tasks, alongside the retained rank-64 result of 3.36/19.80. TUNA results replace EASE results; retained numerical rows in Tables 1–4 are unchanged. Appendix timing plots also exchange their training/inference assignment.

T1.justification: Proposition 3.1 becomes Remark 3.1, and Equation 3 drops the asserted proportionality between projection error and distribution distance. Appendix A.1 revises the associated derivation, introduces a normalized-target qualification and retains the projection-residual lower bound. This is a localized substantive mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: representation rigidity motivates dual-branch geometric and semantic calibration, yielding efficient and accurate CIL across eight benchmarks. Added controls support these claims without redefining the principal contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of LoRA collapse as rank-dependent brittleness, computational controls as evidence against capacity-driven gains, and DINOv2 substitution as evidence against CLIP-specific dependence and leakage (Appendices A.2, C.3 and D.2). These extend causal attribution considerably. The original three technical limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses rank 64 for the original LoRA pilot, identifies thop and UCF T=10 for computational profiling, and supplies caching/offloading pseudocode. Existing optimizer, learning rate, feature dimensions, hardware, seed list, prompt templates and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for TUNA and DINOv2 and removes the EASE reference. The broader related-work organization and positioning of VILA against iterative and analytic CIL remain substantially unchanged; the switch to author–year citations is stylistic.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose is retained. v2 makes localized terminology and theory/algorithm wording edits, adds Experimental setup and Impact Statement headings, and regroups existing algorithm/template and performance/efficiency appendices. This does not amount to an extensive rewrite of the core narrative.

P2.justification: Conference-style formatting substantially reflows the title, abstract, typography and displays. v2 adds Tables 5–9 and Algorithms 3–4, redraws comparator plots, places the training/inference charts together, and moves the vertically stacked main-text K-sensitivity plot to a horizontal appendix display.

improvement.justification: The new rank, computational-budget and broader component controls improve scrutiny of v1's motivation and efficiency claims, while caching clarifies deployment costs. These benefits are qualified: DINOv2 substitution does not establish the claimed exclusion of pretraining leakage, and Tables 8–9 give unexplained differing DB+UGC results for ImageNet-R T=20 (84.95/89.50 versus 82.78/88.32). The added evidence therefore supports a limited net improvement.
